title: Wall Street closed for Thanksgiving as global stocks rebound
dek: U.S. exchanges are shut today and reopen Friday for a half session ending at 1 p.m. ET. Asia and Europe are bouncing after Wednesday's AI-led selloff, helped by U.S. tariff proposals that came in milder than many feared, while hot inflation data keeps a December Fed hike almost fully priced.
quick: U.S. stock and bond markets are closed for Thanksgiving; stocks reopen Friday with a shortened session ending at 1 p.m. ET.
Wednesday: the Nasdaq fell as much as about 4.5% intraday before closing down 0.6%; the S&P 500 lost 0.25% and the Dow rose 0.3%.
October PCE inflation rose to 3.8% year over year (core 3.3%), and fed funds futures price a December 9 quarter-point hike at well above 90%.
The U.S. proposed new tariffs on 14 trading partners; markets read the caps as less severe than feared, and Europe is up about 1.5% today.
S&P Global put Nvidia's AA credit rating on watch for a possible downgrade over governance and key-person risk after Jensen Huang's return as CEO.
Oil holds near Wednesday's jump after a Houthi claim of an attack on Saudi Arabia's Ras Tanura refinery; gold bounced back from a 14-month low.

blocks.head: Inflation runs hotter, cementing a December rate hike
blocks.what: The Commerce Department said the PCE price index, the Fed's preferred inflation gauge, rose 0.3% in October and 3.8% from a year earlier, up from September's annual pace. Core PCE, which strips out food and energy, rose 3.3% year over year, above the 3.2% forecast and the highest in almost three years, per Advisor Perspectives. The same morning, third-quarter GDP growth was revised up to a 4.3% annual rate from 3.4%, and weekly jobless claims fell to 189,000.
blocks.why: Strong growth plus rising inflation is the mix that pushes the Fed toward higher rates. CME FedWatch data cited by CNBC and others put the odds of a quarter-point hike at the December 8 to 9 meeting at roughly 96% to 98%. That supports the dollar and short-term yields and weighs on rate-sensitive growth stocks.
blocks.watch: The next PCE report is due December 23, after the Fed meets. Before then, the debate is whether the Fed hikes by a quarter point or a half point.

blocks.head: AI stocks whipsaw: a deep intraday rout, then a partial recovery
blocks.what: The Nasdaq fell as much as about 4.5% early Wednesday and the Dow dropped more than 1,000 points before buyers stepped in. By the close, the Nasdaq was down 0.6% at 23,585.80, the S&P 500 was down 0.25% at 7,182.78, and the Dow had turned positive, up 0.3% at 50,182.95. Nvidia closed down nearly 4%, giving back part of Monday's roughly 31% surge after Jensen Huang was reinstated as CEO.
blocks.why: Tech and semiconductor stocks carry the most weight in the major indexes, so swings in Nvidia and other AI names drive the overall market. The VIX volatility index ended near 28, a level that signals traders are paying up for protection. Wednesday's late rebound set the tone for today's gains overseas.
blocks.watch: Friday's half session tends to be very thin, so price moves can be exaggerated in either direction.

blocks.head: U.S. proposes new tariffs on 14 trading partners
blocks.what: The U.S. Trade Representative proposed Section 301 tariffs on 14 economies, including China, the European Union, Japan, South Korea, India, Taiwan, Vietnam and Switzerland, after an eight-month probe into excess manufacturing capacity. Reuters reported a proposed 20% rate for China on top of existing duties; the EU, Japan, South Korea and Switzerland face 15% with some exemptions, and several Southeast Asian countries up to 18%. USTR said rates would be capped at levels agreed in existing trade deals, and a comment period and hearings come first, with duties possible in January 2027.
blocks.why: Because the caps largely match levels already in trade agreements, investors in Europe and Asia treated the plan as less damaging than feared, helping exporters and chipmakers rebound. Higher tariffs would still add to U.S. import costs, which matters for an inflation picture that is already running hot.
blocks.watch: Watch the Federal Register notice for the formal rates and the reaction from Beijing and Brussels.

blocks.head: Nvidia's credit rating put on watch for a downgrade
blocks.what: S&P Global Ratings placed Nvidia's AA rating on CreditWatch with negative implications, citing rising management and governance risk and heavy reliance on CEO Jensen Huang, per Reuters and other outlets. S&P said the CEO's exit and quick reinstatement left questions about board oversight of its code of conduct. Moody's, by contrast, said Huang's return reduces near-term uncertainty. The concern is governance, not finances: Nvidia holds more cash than debt.
blocks.why: A one-notch cut would have little direct effect on Nvidia's borrowing costs, but it keeps governance questions in the headlines for the market's most influential stock. Any further fallout tends to ripple through chip stocks and AI-linked names worldwide.
blocks.watch: S&P typically resolves a CreditWatch within about 90 days.

blocks.head: Anthropic shares hover near their IPO price
blocks.what: Anthropic, which priced its IPO at $83 a share last week and raised about $93.5 billion, has traded below or near that price this week after opening its first day at $111.50. Reports put Wednesday's close around $79 to $83, with outlets differing on the exact figure. Some analysts remain positive; Needham has a $150 price target and Wedbush $120, per Fortune.
blocks.why: The stock is being watched as a gauge of investor appetite for AI. CNBC and the New York Times note a weak debut can weigh on other AI names and could slow the pace of startup funding and future tech IPOs.

blocks.text: Asia

Asian markets bounced after Wednesday's sharp losses, though they gave back much of their early gains. Japan's Nikkei 225 rose about 0.9% to roughly 57,500 after being up around 2% early, led by chip and metals stocks; memory maker Kioxia jumped more than 12% on news of work with Nvidia. South Korea's Kospi ended only about 0.3% higher after a drop of more than 6% the day before. Hong Kong's Hang Seng gained about 1.2% to 22,226, recovering from its lowest level since April 2025, while the Shanghai Composite was flat near 3,476. Note the live table may show earlier, intraday levels.

The Bank of Korea raised its benchmark rate by a quarter point to 3.25%, the highest in two years, as economists expected. It cited persistent inflation, strong chip-driven exports and household debt, and it raised its growth forecast. Even after today's bounce, Korea's market is down about 16% this month and Japan's about 8%, per ABC News Australia.
Europe

European stocks are having one of their better days in weeks. By midday, the Stoxx 600 was up about 1.6%, Germany's DAX about 1.9%, France's CAC 40 about 1.8% and the FTSE 100 about 1.6%. Technology shares led, with the region's tech index up about 2.4%, and banks also rose. Traders cited the milder-than-feared U.S. tariff caps and lower bond yields. Wednesday's selloff had pushed the Stoxx 600 near a two-month low, so part of this is a rebound.
Currencies

The dollar is steady in holiday trading. The dollar index is near 104, just below Monday's 20-month high of about 104.6, supported by expectations of further Fed hikes. The euro is around $1.096 as traders look to European Central Bank meeting minutes for clues on December. The yen is weak near 159 per dollar, close to the 160 level where Tokyo stepped in earlier this year, because the gap between U.S. and Japanese interest rates remains wide. The pound is near $1.31, and China's yuan is near 6.66 per dollar.

Cash markets are closed, but stock index futures are trading on a limited holiday schedule. S&P 500 futures were up about 0.7% this morning and Nasdaq 100 futures roughly 1%, extending Wednesday's late recovery. Holiday futures trade on very light volume, so these moves say little about where Friday's session will open.

Wednesday's action shows how fragile sentiment is: the market dropped hard on inflation, tariff and AI valuation worries, then recovered most of the loss by the close. Smaller companies did better, with the Russell 2000 up 0.7%, while the tech-heavy Nasdaq lagged. The VIX rose about 7% to around 28.

Treasury yields fell Wednesday even though the inflation data ran hot, as investors bought bonds for safety during the stock rout, per CNBC. The 2-year yield slipped about 2 basis points to 4.65%, the 10-year fell about 4 basis points to roughly 4.86%, and the 30-year dropped about 4 basis points to about 5.25%. The curve is upward sloping: the 10-year sits roughly 21 basis points above the 2-year, and the 30-year about 39 basis points above the 10-year. The bond market is closed today.

The Fed's target range is 3.75% to 4.00%. Futures markets imply a quarter-point hike at the December 8 to 9 meeting is close to certain, which would lift the range to 4.00% to 4.25%. The open question is size: Governor Christopher Waller said earlier this month that a half-point move is probably needed, while Chair Kevin Warsh has avoided giving that kind of advance guidance, according to reports. Futures still favor a quarter point. JPMorgan economists expect further quarter-point hikes in January and March.
The Fed's Beige Book, released Wednesday, found eight of 12 districts reporting slight to moderate growth, down from nine, and said wage and benefit pressures picked up for hard-to-fill jobs.
Fed speakers today

items: None scheduled; markets and the Fed are off for Thanksgiving.

blocks.text: Wednesday was a split day under the surface. Materials led the S&P 500 sectors, up about 2%, followed by real estate, communication services and industrials, each up close to 1%. Financials and energy also gained about 0.7%. Technology was the weakest sector, down about 0.8%, as Nvidia and other AI-linked names fell, followed by health care, down about 0.6%, and consumer discretionary, down about 0.2%.

The pattern reflects a rotation: investors trimmed the crowded AI trade and moved toward cyclical and value sectors, while lower Treasury yields helped real estate. Several large tech names, including Apple and Meta, finished higher after the early slide, per wire reports.
Names to watch Friday

items: Nvidia: governance headlines and the S&P credit watch remain in focus after a volatile week.
Anthropic: trading around its $83 IPO price, seen as a read on AI demand among investors.
Retailers: Black Friday kicks off the holiday season; Adobe forecasts $12.9 billion in U.S. online Black Friday spending, up 9.2%.
Chinese ADRs such as Li Auto: Li Auto's third-quarter results beat revenue estimates, but its fourth-quarter outlook disappointed, per reports.
Defense and energy stocks: Middle East tensions and oil prices remain a driver.

blocks.text: Oil

Brent crude rose about 3.5% Wednesday to near $94.60 a barrel and U.S. crude about 2% to near $83.70, per CNBC, after Yemen's Houthis said they attacked Saudi Arabia's Ras Tanura refinery, the kingdom's largest. Saudi-led coalition forces said they intercepted drones there and did not confirm damage, but satellite images reviewed by Reuters showed large plumes of smoke. Prices are edging higher again today, with Brent around $95. Offsetting the risk premium, the International Energy Agency expects the oil market to swing back to surplus. OPEC+ ministers meet November 29 to set 2027 output policy.
Gold

Gold briefly fell below $3,500 an ounce Wednesday for the first time since September 2025, as the hot inflation data reinforced expectations of Fed hikes, which make non-yielding gold less attractive. It has since recovered to around $3,580. Recent selling was also tied to investors raising cash to cover losses elsewhere during the AI stock slide, according to reports.
Crypto

Bitcoin is trading around $60,000 to $61,000, steadier today after recent declines, with crypto investment funds still seeing outflows, per FXStreet. Ether is near $1,700. Both remain sensitive to risk appetite in tech stocks and to expectations of higher interest rates.
There are no U.S. economic releases today because of the Thanksgiving holiday. Global markets will take cues from overseas data and headlines instead.

items: Thursday: U.S. markets closed; European markets open with ECB meeting minutes in focus.
Friday 8:30 a.m. ET: advance goods trade balance (forecast about -$135.9 billion) and preliminary wholesale inventories (forecast +0.5%). Both are typically low-impact.
Friday 1:00 p.m. ET: early close for U.S. stock markets.

blocks.text: With U.S. markets closed, there are no major S&P 500 reports today. The busiest names this week are overseas or have already reported.

rows: Q3 revenue of about 28.8 billion yuan beat estimates and the loss narrowed, but Q4 guidance missed expectations; first U.S. trading reaction comes Friday.
No earnings, but early holiday sales reads from Adobe and others set the tone for retail stocks.

blocks.text: The rest of the week is short. U.S. stocks reopen Friday for a half session ending at 1 p.m. ET, with minor trade and inventory data before the open. Black Friday kicks off the holiday shopping season; the National Retail Federation forecasts November and December sales up 4.2% to about $1.01 trillion, with part of the gain coming from higher prices. Over the weekend, OPEC+ meets on November 29 to set 2027 output, which could move oil. Looking further out, the big event is the Fed's December 8 to 9 meeting, where a rate hike is widely expected, while investors track tariff hearings, Middle East tensions and whether AI stocks can stabilize after a volatile November.

bottom_line: Global markets are rebounding on a quiet U.S. holiday as tariff fears ease, but hot inflation, a near-certain December Fed hike and swings in AI stocks keep volatility high heading into Friday's shortened session.
